domain.title: Data structures and algorithms
domain.summary: How data is organized in memory and how the cost of working with it grows as inputs grow.

concepts.title: Arrays and lists
concepts.summary: Ordered collections that support indexed access and iteration; the default structure for sequences of data.
learningObjectives: Trace common array transformations such as map, filter, and reduce
Explain the cost of inserting or removing at the front versus the end
Identify when a linear scan over a list becomes a performance concern
recognitionSignals: find, findIndex, or indexOf results used without handling the not-found case (undefined or -1)
inserting or removing at the front or middle of an array or list: shift, unshift, splice, insert(0, ...), pop(0)
index arithmetic such as i + 1, length - 1, or slice bounds
reduce or accumulator loops over arrays that may be empty
misconceptionPatterns: Assuming includes, find, or indexOf are constant-time lookups
Treating indexOf's -1 not-found result as falsy, or a found index of 0 as not found
Believing reduce without an initial value is safe on an empty array
Believing slice and splice both leave the original array unchanged

concepts.title: Maps and sets
concepts.summary: Key-based structures, usually hash tables, that answer 'have I seen this key?' and 'what value belongs to this key?' in expected constant time; sorted tree-based maps trade that for ordered keys and logarithmic lookup.
learningObjectives: Choose between an array, a set, and a map for a lookup-heavy task
Explain how key equality works for objects versus strings
Refactor a nested-loop lookup into a map-based lookup
recognitionSignals: new Map() or new Set()
objects used as dictionaries keyed by ID
deduplication logic
groupBy or index-building code
misconceptionPatterns: Expecting object or array keys in a Map or Set to be matched by their contents rather than by reference
Assuming every map or dictionary iterates in insertion order (true for JavaScript Map and Python dict, false for Go maps, Java HashMap, Postgres jsonb keys, and integer-like keys on plain JS objects)
Believing a plain JavaScript object is a safe dictionary for arbitrary user-supplied keys such as __proto__ or constructor

concepts.title: Stacks and queues
concepts.summary: Structures that define processing order: last-in-first-out for stacks, first-in-first-out for queues.
learningObjectives: Distinguish LIFO and FIFO processing and predict output order
Trace an iterative traversal that uses an explicit stack, and predict how the visit order changes when the stack is swapped for a queue
Explain why dequeuing from the front of a plain array slows down as the queue grows, and name a structure that avoids it
recognitionSignals: an array or list used as a LIFO stack via push/pop (append/pop)
an in-process array, deque, or queue drained in FIFO order via shift/dequeue/popleft
an explicit stack or queue replacing recursion in traversal code
undo/redo history, bracket or tag matching, or in-process work lists processed in order
misconceptionPatterns: Confusing stack order with queue order, e.g. expecting push/pop to process items in arrival order
Believing an array-backed queue that dequeues with shift stays cheap as the queue grows
Believing that replacing recursion with an explicit stack removes the memory cost of deeply nested input, rather than moving it from the call stack to the heap

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.summary: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances until it reaches a base case.
learningObjectives: Identify the base case and the progress toward it
Trace a recursive call on a small input
Explain the risk of stack overflow on deep or untrusted inputs
recognitionSignals: a function that calls itself
tree or nested JSON traversal
divide-and-conquer helpers
mutual recursion between functions
misconceptionPatterns: Believing Node.js (V8) or Python optimizes tail calls, so a tail-recursive function cannot overflow the stack
Assuming every input eventually reaches the base case, overlooking cyclic references or values that move away from it
Assuming recursion depth is safe because typical inputs are shallow, when nesting depth is controlled by users

concepts.title: Time and space complexity
concepts.summary: Big-O describes how work and memory grow with input size, which predicts where code will fall over at scale.
learningObjectives: Estimate the time complexity of nested loops and chained collection operations
Explain why an O(n²) algorithm can be fine for small n and catastrophic for large n
Identify hidden linear work inside a loop, such as includes or spread-copying an accumulator
recognitionSignals: nested loops over two input-sized collections
find, includes, or indexOf called inside a loop or map/filter callback
copying or spreading an accumulator on every iteration, e.g. reduce((acc, x) => ({ ...acc, ... }))
materializing a whole input-sized result (file, response, or row set) in memory before processing it
misconceptionPatterns: Treating Big-O as a measure of actual runtime
Ignoring memory growth when counting only time
Assuming library calls are constant time

concepts.title: Trees
concepts.summary: Hierarchical structures such as file systems, DOMs, ASTs, and B-tree indexes, traversed depth-first or breadth-first.
learningObjectives: Trace depth-first and breadth-first traversals on a small tree
Explain how tree height affects lookup cost
Recognize tree structures hiding in nested data such as comments or categories
recognitionSignals: parent/children relationships in data
recursive rendering of nested components
AST or DOM walking
self-referencing foreign keys
misconceptionPatterns: Assuming nested data such as comments or categories is always shallow
Assuming parent/child data loaded from a database or user input is guaranteed acyclic, so traversal needs no visited set or depth limit
Believing every tree gives logarithmic lookup regardless of balance

concepts.title: Searching and sorting
concepts.summary: Ordering data and finding items in it efficiently, including binary search and stable comparison-based sorting.
learningObjectives: Explain why binary search requires sorted input
Predict the outcome of a custom comparator, including stability
Choose between sorting in the database and sorting in application code
recognitionSignals: sort calls with comparator functions or sort keys
sorting, filtering, or top-N selection in application code on rows that were already fetched
binary search, bisect, or lower-bound helpers
string ordering using localeCompare, collation, or case normalization
misconceptionPatterns: Believing default JavaScript sort compares numbers numerically
Believing a comparator may return a boolean instead of a negative, zero, or positive number
Assuming a query without ORDER BY returns rows in insertion or primary-key order
Believing binary search over unsorted or differently sorted data will fail loudly rather than silently return a wrong result
